# Vitamins

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Basics of endocrinology and metabolism > Vitamins*

[Original Article Link](/library/Ao0ReS)

---

## Summary

Vitamins are a group of chemically diverse organic compounds that an organism requires for normal metabolism. Apart from a few exceptions (e.g., <u>vitamin D</u>), the human body cannot synthesize vitamins on its own in sufficient amounts and must, therefore, ensure a steady supply through the diet. Vitamins are <u>micronutrients</u> that do not provide energy (like <u>macronutrients</u>) but instead have very specific biochemical roles. They can be <u>coenzymes</u> in various reactions (<u>B vitamins</u>, vitamins A and K) and/or antioxidants that protect <u>the cell</u> and its membrane from <u>free radicals</u> (vitamins C and E). They can also enable <u>cell signaling</u> (<u>vitamin A</u>) and <u>gene transcription</u> (vitamins A and E) or function as <u>hormones</u> (e.g., <u>vitamin D</u>). Vitamins are classified into <u>fat-soluble vitamins</u>, which the body can store, and <u>water-soluble vitamins</u>, which, with the exception of vitamins B<sub>9</sub> (<u>folate</u>) and B<sub>12</sub> (<u>cobalamin</u>), the body cannot store over significant periods of time and, therefore, require continuous intake. A balanced diet typically supplies the body with all vitamins it requires. Deficiencies occur mainly due to <u>malnutrition</u>, <u>malabsorption</u> disorders, or restrictive diets (e.g., <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u> in a <u>vegan diet</u>).




See also "<u>Cutaneous manifestations of nutritional deficiencies</u>."

| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Fat-soluble vitamins</u> | <u>Water-soluble vitamins</u> |

| Sources | <br><br>* Diet (except <u>vitamin D</u> which is predominantly synthesized in the body)<br><br>* Intestinal flora: small amounts of <u>vitamin K</u> are synthesized by intestinal bacteria<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Mainly diet<br><br>* Intestinal flora: small amounts of <u>vitamin B<sub>7</sub></u>, B<sub>9</sub>, and B<sub>12</sub> are synthesized by intestinal bacteria<br><br><br> |
| Absorption | <br><br>* Absorption depends on intestinal and <u>pancreatic</u> function<br><br>* Require lipids for absorption<br><br><br> | <br>* Absorption in the intestine via specific luminal transporters<br><br> |
| Storage | <br>* Can be stored for long periods of time in the <u>liver</u> and <u>adipose tissue</u><br><br> | <br>* Not stored in the body, except vitamins B<sub>9</sub> and B<sub>12</sub>, which are stored in the <u>liver</u><br><br>* B<sub>9</sub> stores last for approx. 3–4 months.<br><br>* B<sub>12</sub> stores last for approx. 3–4 years<br><br> |
| Functions | <br>* Function primarily as<br><br>* <u>Hormones</u> (<u>vitamin D</u>)<br><br>* Antioxidants (e.g., <u>vitamin E</u>)<br><br>* <u>Cell signaling</u> (e.g., <u>vitamin A</u>)<br><br>* <u>Gene transcription</u> (e.g., vitamins A and E)<br><br> | <br>* Function primarily as<br><br>* <u>Coenzymes</u> (e.g., <u>ascorbic acid</u>)<br><br>* Precursors to <u>coenzymes</u> in chemical reactions (e.g., <u>NAD<sup>+</sup></u>, <u>FAD</u>)<br><br>* Antioxidants (<u>vitamin C</u>)<br><br> |
| Vitamin deficiency | <br>* Causes include<br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u><br><br>* <u>Steatorrhea</u> caused by <u>malabsorption</u> (e.g., in <u>celiac disease</u> and <u>cystic fibrosis</u>)<br><br>* <u>Bile acid</u> deficiency (e.g., <u>cholestasis</u>, <u>bile acid</u> <u>malabsorption</u>)<br><br>* Medications or supplements (e.g., <u>orlistat</u>, mineral oil)<br><br>* Genetic disorders (e.g., hereditary forms of <u>rickets</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Causes include<br><br>* Restricted diet (e.g., <u>vegan diet</u>)<br><br>* <u>Malabsorption</u> disorder (e.g., <u>gastritis</u>, following gastric resection)<br><br>* Congenital disorders (e.g., <u>Hartnup disease</u>)<br><br>* Deficiency of B-complex can cause glossitis, dermatitis, and <u>diarrhea</u><br><br><br> |
| Vitamin toxicity | <br><br>* Oversupplementation → accumulation in adipose tissue → toxic excess<br><br>* <u>Vitamin toxicity</u> occurs more often than with water-soluble vitamins (see respective sections below)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Accumulation and subsequent toxicity are very rare (<u>kidneys</u> detect and remove excess in urine).<br><br>* No toxicity has been described for vitamins B<sub>1</sub>, B<sub>2</sub>, B<sub>5</sub>, <u>B<sub>7</sub></u>, B<sub>9</sub>, and B<sub>12</sub>.<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Accumulation and toxicity occur almost exclusively with <u>fat-soluble vitamins</u>.

## Vitamin A (retinol)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>retinol</u>

* Substance class: <u>retinoids</u>

* Chemical structure: isoprenoid

* Inactive precursors (provitamins): carotenoids (esp., alpha-<u>carotene</u>, <u>beta-carotene</u>, gamma-<u>carotene</u>)

* Activation: carotinoid is cleaved into two retinal molecules; it can be reversibly reduced to <u>retinol</u> and reversibly oxidized to <u>retinoic acid</u>

* Active forms

* Retinal

* <u>Retinoic acid</u>

* Sources

* Plant sources; : as inactive provitamin (esp. <u>beta-carotene</u>) in yellow and leafy vegetables (e.g., spinach, kale, carrots)

* Animal sources: in storage form;  (e.g., in <u>liver</u>, <u>kidney</u>, fish, eggs, butter)

* Transport: via transport <u>proteins</u> (in the form of <u>retinol</u>)

* Cellular <u>retinoic acid</u>-binding (<u>CRAB</u>) protein: selectively binds <u>retinoic acid</u>

* Retinol-binding protein: <u>retinol</u> transport vehicle in serum

* Storage

* In hepatic cells;  (<u>Ito cells</u>) within the <u>perisinusoidal space</u> (of Disse)

* Storage form: retinyl ester (e.g., retinyl <u>palmitate</u>)

* Excretion: via <u>bile</u> and urine





### Functions




* <u>Vision</u>: component of <u>rhodopsin</u> as 11-cis-retinal

* <u>Gene transcription</u>

* <u>All-trans retinoic acid</u> (<u>ATRA</u>) binds to its <u>nuclear receptors</u>;  (retinoic acid receptors, RAR; <u>retinoid</u> X <u>receptors</u>, RXR) → <u>receptor</u> dimerization → binding to <u>DNA</u>;  → uncoiling of <u>chromatin</u> → exposure of <u>promoter</u> regions of <u>genes</u> → binding of <u>transcription factors</u> to <u>promoter</u> → <u>initiation of transcription</u> and <u>cell differentiation</u>

* Regulation of various <u>genes</u> responsible for cell growth, <u>cell differentiation</u>, <u>apoptosis</u>, reproduction (e.g., <u>spermatogenesis</u>), and <u>embryonic development</u>

* <u>Vitamin A</u> production in the intestine is controlled by a <u>homeobox</u> <u>transcription factor</u>. [[1]](/library/uxWpyn0)

* Tissue maintenance and <u>cell differentiation</u>

* Mainly <u>retinoic acid</u>

* Promotes differentiation of <u>epithelium</u> into specialized tissue (e.g., <u>pancreatic</u> cells and <u>goblet cells</u>)

* Prevents <u>metaplasia</u> of squamous cells

* Antioxidant





> [!NOTE]
> Retinal is a major component of the retinal pigment <u>rhodopsin</u> in rods, which is necessary for <u>vision</u>, while <u>retinoic acid</u> and <u>retinol</u> are involved mainly in <u>gene transcription</u> and tissue maintenance.




> [!NOTE]
> Retinol (vitamin A) nurtures the retinA, acts as an Antioxidant, and can be used for Acne treatment.




![Section 20.10 Vitamin A](media/small_62f22654c787e5.87072917.jpg)

Section 20.10 Vitamin A




### Vitamin A deficiency [[2]](/library/BR0z6f)




* Causes

* Disorders associated with fat <u>malabsorption</u>: <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u> (e.g., <u>Crohn disease</u>), <u>celiac disease</u>, <u>cystic fibrosis</u>, <u>pancreatic</u> insufficiency, <u>cholestasis</u>[[3]](/library/yR0dpf)

* <u>Malnutrition</u>: most common cause of <u>vitamin A deficiency</u> in developing countries

* Clinical features

* Ocular manifestations

* Night blindness (<u>nyctalopia</u>)

* <u>Retinopathy</u>

* <u>Xerophthalmia</u>

* Keratomalacia

* Bitot spots: gray, triangular, dry patches on the bulbar <u>conjunctiva</u>, covered by a layer with a foamy appearance  

* Typical sign of <u>vitamin A</u> deficiency

* Caused by squamous cell <u>metaplasia</u> and <u>keratinization</u> of the <u>conjunctiva</u>

* Keratinizing squamous <u>metaplasia</u> of the <u>bladder</u> (pearl-like <u>plaques</u> on <u>cystoscopy</u>)

* <u>Xerosis cutis</u>

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>: <u>Vitamin A</u> deficiency increases the risk of a <u>measles</u> infection taking a severe course.

* Poor growth





![Vitamin A deficiency](media/jpf38bd8njn7kyo4lk1w6rxl.jpg)

Vitamin A deficiency

![Bitot spot](media/f1vwpfv1q0d68ws4gp0fwbf5.jpg)

Bitot spot




### Vitamin A toxicity




* Causes: increased intake via supplements or drugs

* Clinical features

* Acute toxicity

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Vertigo</u>

* Fatigue

* <u>Headache</u>

* Blurred <u>vision</u>

* Chronic toxicity

* <u>Alopecia</u>

* <u>Arthralgias</u>

* Dry <u>skin</u>, <u>scaling</u>

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>, hepatic toxicity

* <u>Pseudotumor cerebri</u>

* <u>Teratogenic</u> effects

* Facial anomalies: <u>microcephaly</u>, <u>microphthalmia</u>; , and <u>cleft palate</u>

* <u>Thymic</u> <u>agenesis</u>

* Cardiovascular abnormalities

* Neurodevelopmental disability

* Fetal <u>death</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic. A negative <u>pregnancy test</u> and two forms of <u>contraception</u> are required before prescribing isoretinoin to women.




### Therapeutic uses [[4]](/library/d3YohK)




<u>Vitamin A</u> is contraindicated in <u>pregnancy</u> (<u>teratogenic</u>): A negative <u>pregnancy test</u> and two forms of <u>contraception</u> must be provided before <u>isotretinoin</u> can be prescribed to women.




* <u>Measles</u>; : Treatment with <u>vitamin A</u> is recommended for all individuals with <u>vitamin A deficiency</u>,;  since it reduces complications and mortality.  [[5]](/library/U3Yb3K)[[6]](/library/23YT3K)

* <u>Skin</u> conditions

* Severe <u>cystic acne</u> (e.g., nodulocystic) and <u>rosacea</u>: <u>isotretinoin</u> (13-cis-retinoic acid) PO

* <u>Mild acne</u>: topical <u>vitamin A</u>

* <u>Acute promyelocytic leukemia</u>: all-trans <u>retinoic acid</u> (<u>ATRA</u>)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Vitamin A</u> should be given to <u>measles</u> patients with <u>vitamin A</u> deficiency to boost their <u>immune system</u> and reduce the risk of complications and mortality, especially in countries where <u>vitamin A</u> deficiency is <u>endemic</u>.

## Vitamin D (calciferol)

### Characteristics




* Substance class: <u>steroid hormones</u>, calciferols

* Active form: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25-(OH)2 D<sub>3</sub>, <u>calcitriol</u>)

* Sources:

* Ergocalciferol (<u>vitamin D<sub>2</sub></u>): mushrooms, fortified foods;  (e.g., milk, breakfast cereals, formula), <u>yeast</u> (from <u>ergosterol</u>)

* Cholecalciferol (<u>vitamin D<sub>3</sub></u>)

* Synthesized in the <u>skin</u> (<u>stratum basale</u>) when exposed to <u>UV light</u>

* Fortified foods;  (e.g., milk; , breakfast cereals, formula), fatty fish;  (<u>liver</u>), egg yolks, plants

* Vitamin D synthesis 
1. * <u>Liver</u>: <u>cholesterol</u> → 7-dehydrocholesterol (provitamin D<sub>3</sub>)
* Enzyme: <u>cholesterol</u> <u>dehydrogenase</u>
2. * <u>Skin</u>

* Storage of <u>7-dehydrocholesterol</u>

* Cleavage of <u>7-dehydrocholesterol</u> via <u>irradiation</u> with <u>UV light</u> → <u>cholecalciferol</u> (in the <u>stratum basale</u>)
3. * <u>Liver</u>: <u>hydroxylation</u> of <u>cholecalciferol</u> to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OH D3, <u>calcidiol</u>)
4. * <u>Kidneys</u>: 1α-hydroxylase <u>hydroxylates</u> <u>25-hydroxyvitamin D</u> → <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u>

* Transport to <u>target cells</u>: vitamin D-binding protein (<u>DBP</u>)

* Storage: as <u>25-hydroxycholecalciferol</u>, mainly in <u>adipose tissue</u>;  (25-OH D<sub>3</sub>)

* Regulation of <u>vitamin D synthesis</u>: via regulation of <u>1α-hydroxylase</u> activity in <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u> 

* ↓ <u>Calcium</u>, ↓ <u>phosphate</u>, and ↑ <u>PTH</u> → ↑ <u>1α-hydroxylase</u> activity → ↑ <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> biosynthesis

* ↑ <u>Calcium</u>, ↑ <u>phosphate</u>, and ↑ <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> (feedback inhibition) → ↓ <u>1α-hydroxylase</u> activity → ↓ <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> biosynthesis





> [!TIP]
> <u>Vitamin D</u> is the only vitamin that the human body can produce entirely on its own!




![Biosynthesis of vitamin D](media/mjvnxb5oarxn9eusblu50umk.jpg)

Biosynthesis of vitamin D




### Functions




* <u>Calcium</u> and <u>phosphate</u> metabolism (see “<u>Calcium homeostasis</u>.”)

* ↑ Absorption of <u>calcium</u> and <u>phosphate</u> in the intestine

* ↑ Reabsorption of <u>calcium</u> in the <u>kidneys</u>

* Stimulation of bone mineralization and remodeling (at low <u>vitamin D</u> levels)

* Indirectly: through maintenance of serum <u>calcium</u> and <u>phosphate</u> levels

* Directly: through activation of <u>osteoblasts</u> and promotion of <u>osteoclast</u> differentiation

* Bone resorption (at high <u>vitamin D</u> levels)





![Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism](media/m1mufp2p8vmqt0ihbo0mz73r.jpg)

Regulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism

![Section 20.11 Vitamin D](media/small_62f226936e4428.05964446.jpg)

Section 20.11 Vitamin D




### Deficiency [[7]](/library/AR0Rpf)




* Most commonly because of a lack of sun exposure;  (particularly high risk of deficiency in heavily pigmented <u>skin</u> and use of sunscreen due to inhibition of <u>vitamin D</u> synthesis) )

* May cause:

* In adults: <u>osteomalacia</u>

* In children: <u>rickets</u>

* Symptoms of <u>hypocalcemia</u>;  (e.g., <u>tetany</u>)

* For more information see “<u>Vitamin D deficiency</u>.”





![Rickets of the lower extremities](media/pcyukew0os7np6mlauc5ksep.jpg)

Rickets of the lower extremities




### Vitamin D toxicity




* Causes

* Oversupplementation

* Granulomatous disorders (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>): due to increased <u>1α-hydroxylase</u> activation in epithelioid <u>macrophages</u> → increased <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> synthesis

* Clinical features

* <u>Hypercalcemia</u>, <u>hypercalciuria</u> (see also <u>laboratory evaluation of bone disease</u>)

* Loss of appetite

* <u>Stupor</u>





### Therapeutic uses




* <u>Osteoporosis</u> (prevention and treatment)

* Paget disease

* Prenatal supplementation for <u>vegetarian</u> mothers (400 IU per day)

## Vitamin E (tocopherol)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: : <u>tocopherol</u>, <u>tocotrienol</u>

* Substance class: tocopherols

* Chemical structure: chromane with isoprenoid side chain

* Inactive precursors (provitamins): none

* Active form: <u>tocopherol</u>

* Sources: meat, eggs, vegetable oils, leafy vegetables [[8]](/library/zR0rpf)

* Transport: <u>alpha-tocopherol transfer protein</u> (α-TTP)

* Storage: <u>adipose tissue</u>, <u>parenchymal</u> cells of the <u>liver</u>

* Excretion: via <u>bile</u>





### Functions




* Antioxidant

* Prevents <u>free radical damage</u>, especially in <u>RBCs</u> and at <u>cell membranes</u>

* Interrupts <u>free radical</u> chains and oxidizes itself as a result

* Other functions

* Inhibition of <u>platelet aggregation</u>, cell <u>proliferation</u>, and <u>monocyte</u> adhesion

* <u>Enzyme inhibition</u> (e.g., protein <u>kinase</u> C, <u>phospholipase A2</u>)

* Inhibition of <u>gene transcription</u> (e.g., for <u>α-TTP</u>, <u>tropomyosin</u> alpha-1 chain)





![Section 20.12 Vitamin E](media/small_62f226df3f3c50.08664087.jpg)

Section 20.12 Vitamin E




### Vitamin E deficiency




* Deficiency is very rare.

* Causes [[8]](/library/zR0rpf)

* Fat <u>malabsorption</u> disorders (e.g., <u>cystic fibrosis</u>)

* Defects in <u>genes</u> that code for <u>α-TTP</u>

* Clinical features

* Neurologic dysfunction

* <u>Demyelination</u> of the <u>posterior column</u> and <u>spinocerebellar</u> tract → ↓ <u>proprioception</u> and vibration sensation; <u>ataxia</u> (mimics <u>Friedreich ataxia</u>)

* Neurologic symptoms are similar to <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> deficiency, except that <u>vitamin E</u> deficiency does not lead to <u>hypersegmented neutrophils</u>, <u>megaloblastic anemia</u>, and increased <u>methylmalonic acid</u> levels. [[9]](/library/ai0QJf)

* <u>Hemolytic anemia</u>; : deficiency results in increased fragility of <u>erythrocytes</u> and membrane breakdown [[8]](/library/zR0rpf)

* <u>Acanthocytosis</u>

* <u>Muscle weakness</u>





### Vitamin E toxicity




* Toxicity is very rare.

* Causes: oversupplementation

* Clinical features

* In <u>infants</u>: increased risk of <u>necrotizing enterocolitis</u> (<u>NEC</u>)

* High-dose supplementation: alteration of <u>vitamin K</u> metabolism → ↑ anticoagulatory effects of <u>warfarin</u> → ↑ risk of bleeding

* Increased <u>incidence</u> of <u>heart failure</u>, <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>, and increased mortality [[10]](/library/V3YGhK)





### Therapeutic uses



* <u>Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis</u>: consider <u>vitamin E</u> for antioxidant effect

---

## Vitamin K (phytomenadione)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms

* Vitamin K<sub>1</sub> (<u>phytomenadione</u>, <u>phytonadione</u>, or <u>phylloquinone</u>)

* Vitamin K<sub>2</sub> (menaquinone)

* Substance class: naphthoquinones

* Chemical structure:

* Vitamin K1

* Vitamin K2

* Inactive precursors (provitamins): none

* Active form: <u>vitamin K</u> hydroquinone

* Activation occurs via enzyme epoxide reductase.

* Mutations in the VKORC1 (<u>Vitamin K</u> epOxide Reductase Complex subunit 1) <u>gene</u> impair the reduction of <u>vitamin K</u> <u>epoxide</u>, resulting in deficiencies in <u>vitamin K</u>-dependent <u>clotting factors</u>.

* Sources

* Leafy green vegetables (vitamin K<sub>1</sub>)

* Eggs, dairy, and meat (vitamin K<sub>2</sub>)

* Synthesized in small amounts by intestinal bacteria

* Transport: via <u>lipoproteins</u>; no specific protein

* Storage: <u>liver</u>

* Excretion: <u>bile</u> and urine





### Functions



* <u>Cofactor</u> for γ-<u>carboxylation</u> of <u>glutamate</u> residues on <u>vitamin-K</u>-dependent <u>proteins</u> involved in:

* Coagulation: maturation of <u>factors II</u> (<u>prothrombin</u>), VII, IX, and X, <u>protein C</u>, <u>protein S</u>

* Bone formation: <u>osteocalcin</u> (bone <u>Gla</u> protein), matrix <u>Gla</u> protein




> [!NOTE]
> Koagulation requires Vitamin K.









![Section 20.13 Vitamin K](media/small_62f22713f27453.36698078.jpg)

Section 20.13 Vitamin K




### Vitamin K deficiency [[11]](/library/Yi0nJf)




* Causes

* <u>Liver</u> failure (e.g., <u>cirrhosis</u>)

* Fat <u>malabsorption</u>

* Prolonged broad-spectrum <u>antibiotic therapy</u>

* <u>Vitamin K antagonists</u> (e.g., <u>warfarin</u>)

* Neonatal deficiency

* The neonatal intestine is sterile (no flora to synthesize <u>vitamin K</u>).

* <u>Vitamin K</u> does not cross the <u>placenta</u>.

* <u>Breast milk</u> does not contain <u>vitamin K</u>.

* The neonatal <u>liver</u> is incapable of synthesizing the active form of <u>vitamin K</u>.

* Clinical features

* Hemorrhage (e.g., <u>petechiae</u>, <u>ecchymoses</u>)

* <u>Vitamin K deficiency bleeding</u> (<u>VKDB</u>) 

* ↑ <u>PT</u> and <u>aPTT</u>, normal <u>bleeding time</u>

* Postnatal prophylaxis: <u>vitamin K</u> injection at <u>birth</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Warfarin</u> inhibits the <u>vitamin K</u>-dependent synthesis of <u>clotting factors</u> and <u>proteins</u>.




![Vitamin K deficiency factsheet](media/dzoi3t21nh2brot04n89vcjt.jpg)

Vitamin K deficiency factsheet

![Vitamin-K deficiency bleeding of the newborn factsheet](media/rbverg8qbu06rk4apm7s40by.jpg)

Vitamin-K deficiency bleeding of the newborn factsheet




### Vitamin K toxicity




* Toxicity is very rare.

* Cause: oversupplementation

* Clinical features

* <u>Hemolytic anemia</u>

* <u>Hyperbilirubinemia</u>

* <u>Jaundice</u>

* <u>Kernicterus</u> in <u>infants</u>





### Therapeutic uses




* Postnatal <u>vitamin K</u> injection to prevent <u>VKDB</u>

* <u>Coagulopathy</u>: disorders of the <u>extrinsic pathway of coagulation</u>.

## Vitamin B₁ (thiamine)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>thiamine</u>

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active form: thiamine pyrophosphate (<u>TPP</u>); activation via intracellular <u>phosphorylation</u> of <u>thiamine</u>

* Sources: whole-grain cereals (e.g., whole wheat, brown rice), <u>yeast</u>, pork, legumes [[13]](/library/Si0yIf)

* Resorption: via <u>thiamine</u> transporter-2 (ThTR2)

* Transport in blood: mainly via blood cells; only ∼10% is free or bound to <u>albumin</u>





### Functions



* <u>Cofactor</u> for several enzymes involved in <u>carbohydrate</u> and <u>amino acid metabolism</u>:

* <u>Pyruvate dehydrogenase</u> (connects <u>glycolysis</u> to <u>citric acid cycle</u>): <u>pyruvate</u> → <u>acetyl-CoA</u>

* <u>Alpha-ketoglutaric acid dehydrogenase</u> (<u>citric acid cycle</u>): α-Ketoglutarate → <u>succinyl-CoA</u>

* <u>Transketolase</u> (<u>HMP shunt</u>)

* D-xylulose-5-P ⇄ D-ribose-5-P

* <u>Glyceraldehyde-3-P</u> ⇄ D-xylulose-5-P

* Branched-chain ketoacid <u>dehydrogenase</u>

* <u>Valine</u>/<u>isoleucine</u> → <u>Propionyl-CoA</u>

* <u>Leucine</u> → <u>Acetyl-CoA</u>




> [!NOTE]
> Enzymes <u>thiamine</u> is a <u>cofactor</u> for: <u>Thiamine</u> PATs your Back! (Pyruvate <u>dehydrogenase</u>, Alpha-ketoglutaric acid <u>dehydrogenase</u>, Transketolase, Branched-chain ketoacid <u>dehydrogenase</u>).




![Section 20.1 Thiamine B1](media/small_62f223e3393c94.25944430.jpg)

Section 20.1 Thiamine B1




### Vitamin B<sub>1</sub> deficiency [[14]](/library/fi0kIf)




* Causes

* <u>Heavy drinking</u>

* <u>Malnutrition</u>, <u>starvation</u>

* <u>Malabsorption</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>

* <u>Diarrhea</u>, prolonged <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Diuretics</u>, <u>hemodialysis</u>

* <u>Bariatric surgery</u>

* Pathophysiology

* <u>Thiamine</u> deficiency → impaired <u>glucose</u> breakdown →  <u>ATP</u> depletion → tissue damage that primarily affects highly aerobic tissues (e.g., <u>brain</u>, <u>heart</u>)

* High-dose <u>glucose</u> infusions lead to increased <u>ATP</u> depletion, which can trigger <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u>.
* In <u>malnourished</u> individuals and chronic <u>alcohol</u> users/heavy drinkers, <u>thiamine</u> should be administered before <u>glucose</u> infusions.

* Clinical features

* Beriberi: inadequate <u>thiamine</u> uptake due to <u>malnutrition</u>, <u>heavy drinking</u>, or increased demand (e.g., <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>pregnancy</u>) 

* <u>Dry beriberi</u>

* Symmetrical <u>peripheral neuropathy</u> (sensory and motor)

* Progressive muscle wasting

* <u>Paralysis</u>

* Confusion

* <u>Wet beriberi</u>

* <u>High-output cardiac failure</u> (due to systemic <u>vasodilation</u>)

* <u>Dilated cardiomyopathy</u>

* <u>Cardiomegaly</u>

* <u>Edema</u>

* Infantile beriberi: <u>cardiomegaly</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>cyanosis</u>, <u>aseptic meningitis</u> (<u>vomiting</u> and <u>seizures</u>)

* <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Leigh syndrome</u>

* Diagnostics: <u>vitamin B<sub>1</sub></u> administration → ↑ RBC transketolase activity





> [!TIP]
> In <u>malnourished</u> or <u>alcohol</u>-dependent patients, always administer <u>thiamine</u> before giving dextrose to decrease the risk of precipitating or exacerbating <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Vitamin B1 deficiency causes Ber1Ber1.




![Vitamin B1 deficiency](media/ql6q355pw16bh37rr5mmnt9j.jpg)

Vitamin B1 deficiency

---

## Vitamin B₂ (riboflavin)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>riboflavin</u>

* Substance class: flavins

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active forms: : flavin mononucleotide (<u>FMN</u>), flavin adenine dinucleotide (<u>FAD</u>)

* Sources: meat, fish, eggs, milk, green vegetables, <u>yeast</u>[[13]](/library/Si0yIf)

* Resorption: flavoproteins are cleaved into <u>riboflavin</u>  in the intestine

* Transport in blood: via <u>albumin</u> and <u>immunoglobulins</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Active forms of riboFlavin are FMN and FAD.




### Functions



* <u>FAD</u> and <u>FMN</u> are <u>cofactors</u> for enzymes that are involved in redox reactions (chemical reactions in which electrons are transferred from one substance to another), including:

* <u>Succinate dehydrogenase</u> (<u>TCA cycle</u>)

* <u>FAD</u> is part of glutathione reductase (GR) in <u>erythrocytes</u>: <u>NADPH</u> binds to GR → reduction of <u>FAD</u> to FADH<sup>-</sup> → FADH<sup>-</sup> breaks <u>disulfide bond</u> in <u>GSSG</u> → GSR can be reduced




![Section 20.2 Riboflavin B2](media/small_62f2242cdb96c8.81190389.jpg)

Section 20.2 Riboflavin B2




### Vitamin B<sub>2</sub> deficiency [[15]](/library/gi0FIf)[[16]](/library/e3YxhK)




* Causes

* <u>Malnutrition</u>

* Restricted diet (e.g., <u>vegan</u>, <u>lactose</u>-free)

* ↑ Demand: <u>pregnancy</u>, lactation

* Clinical features

* Corneal vascularization

* <u>Cheilitis</u>, <u>glossitis</u>, <u>stomatitis</u>, <u>pharyngitis</u>

* <u>Normocytic</u> normochromic <u>anemia</u>

* <u>Seborrheic dermatitis</u>

* Diagnosis

* <u>Erythrocyte</u> <u>glutathione reductase</u> assay: identifies subtle deficiencies

* <u>Erythrocyte</u> <u>glutathione reductase</u> activity coefficient: the activity coefficient (AC) of <u>glutathione reductase</u> is measured in the presence and absence of <u>FAD</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The 2 C's of Vitamin B2 deficiency: Corneal vascularization and Cheilitis!




![Angular stomatitis](media/v4kampt0fxon8gc61bc0lk5y.jpg)

Angular stomatitis

---

## Vitamin B₃ (niacin)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>niacin</u>, <u>nicotinic acid</u>

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active forms
* Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (<u>NAD<sup>+</sup></u>/<u>NADH</u>) Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (<u>NADP<sup>+</sup></u>/ <u>NADPH</u>)

* <u>NADPH</u> provides electrons for <u>anabolic</u> reactions (e.g., synthesis of <u>fatty acids</u> and <u>steroids</u>) and oxidation-reduction reactions. Also used in the <u>respiratory burst</u>, the <u>cytochrome P450 system</u>, and <u>glutathione reductase</u>.

* Reduced form is <u>NADPH</u>; oxidized form is <u>NADP<sup>+</sup></u>.





* <u>NAD<sup>+</sup></u> serves as an electron carrier in <u>redox reactions</u>, especially in <u>catabolic</u> cellular processes.

* Reduced form is <u>NADH</u>; oxidized form is <u>NAD<sup>+</sup></u>.

* Sources: meat (<u>liver</u>), cereals, seeds, legumes

* Synthesis:  : derived from <u>tryptophan</u>;  ; requires vitamins B<sub>2</sub> and B<sub>6</sub>

* Resorption: passive resorption in the intestine

* Transport in blood: as nicotinate





![NAD+ / NADH redox pair](media/aag17v7v8z61fsa3fi43r92s.jpg)

NAD+ / NADH redox pair

![Niacin (nicotinic acid)](media/aifrrojlrbi4z2mrd3e6mj18.jpg)

Niacin (nicotinic acid)

![Niacinamide](media/qp7pfdievt8mxua0c67jjati.jpg)

Niacinamide




> [!TIP]
> Active forms of Niacin are NAD+ and N<u>ADP</u>+.




### Functions



* <u>Cofactor</u> for <u>redox reactions</u> (e.g., <u>alcohol dehydrogenase</u>, <u>isocitrate dehydrogenase</u>, <u>G6PD</u>)




![Section 20.3 Niacin B3](media/small_62f22460b56839.26989095.jpg)

Section 20.3 Niacin B3




### Vitamin B<sub>3</sub> deficiency [[13]](/library/Si0yIf)




* Causes

* <u>Malnutrition</u>

* <u>Heavy drinking</u>

* Conditions associated with <u>tryptophan</u> deficiency

* <u>Hartnup disease</u>: decreased renal and intestinal <u>tryptophan</u> absorption

* <u>Carcinoid syndrome</u> (if metabolically active): increased <u>tryptophan</u> metabolism

* <u>Vitamin B<sub>6</sub> deficiency</u> (e.g., due to treatment with <u>isoniazid</u>): decreased <u>niacin</u> synthesis from <u>tryptophan</u>

* Chronic consumption of grains (e.g., <u>corn</u>) that have not been processed by <u>nixtamalization</u> (common cause in developing countries)

* Clinical features  

* <u>Glossitis</u>

* <u>Pellagra</u> (caused by severe deficiency)

* Characteristic dermatitis

* Circular broad collar <u>rash</u> on the neck (Casal necklace); affects <u>dermatomes</u> C3 and C4

* <u>Hyperpigmented</u> <u>skin</u> lesions in sun-exposed areas (especially on the limbs)

* <u>Diarrhea</u> and <u>vomiting</u>

* Neurologic symptoms;  (e.g, <u>dementia</u>, <u>hallucinations</u>, <u>anxiety</u>, <u>insomnia</u>, <u>encephalopathy</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> 3 typical features of severe vitamin B3 Deficiency: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, and Dementia.




![Vitamin B₃ deficiency](media/j8y61h6v6wk52tb6k2rpmd58.jpg)

Vitamin B₃ deficiency

![Pellagra](media/xntdd1wcie403ntmb1u17che.jpg)

Pellagra




### Vitamin B<sub>3</sub> toxicity




* <u>Facial flushing</u>: due to <u>prostaglandin</u> release and NOT due to <u>histamine</u>;  (typically seen when <u>niacin</u> therapy is started, can be avoided by coadministration of <u>aspirin</u>)  [[17]](/library/u5YpNp)

* <u>Hyperuricemia</u>, <u>podagra</u>

* <u>Hyperglycemia</u>

* Possibly: <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>pruritus</u>, <u>hives</u> [[12]](/library/85YONp)





### Therapeutic use



* <u>Dyslipidemia</u>: <u>Niacin</u> lowers <u>VLDL</u> and increases <u>HDL</u> serum levels (see “<u>Second-line lipid-lowering agents</u>”).




![Dyslipidemia - Part 4: Laboratory Parameters & Lipid-Lowering Agents](media/small_5f745f08b5846.jpg)

Dyslipidemia - Part 4: Laboratory Parameters & Lipid-Lowering Agents

---

## Vitamin B₅ (pantothenic acid)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>pantothenic acid</u>, <u>pantothenate</u>

* Substance class: carboxylic acid

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active forms: <u>pantothenic acid</u>

* Sources: <u>liver</u>, <u>kidney</u>, egg yolks, broccoli, milk

* Transport in blood: bound to <u>proteins</u>





### Functions



* Essential component of coenzyme A (<u>pantothenic acid</u> + <u>ADP</u> + <u>cysteine</u>)

* <u>Cofactor</u> for the transfer of acyl groups → activation of carboxylic acids (e.g., <u>pyruvate dehydrogenase</u>, <u>α-ketoglutarate</u> <u>dehydrogenase</u>)

* <u>Cofactor</u> for <u>fatty acid</u>, <u>cholesterol</u>, and <u>acetylcholine</u> synthesis




![Section 20.4 Pantothenic Acid B5](media/small_62f224a20ecca3.68447979.jpg)

Section 20.4 Pantothenic Acid B5




### Vitamin B<sub>5</sub> deficiency [[13]](/library/Si0yIf)




Deficiency is rare.




* Causes: <u>malnutrition</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Adrenal insufficiency</u>; may lead to <u>distal</u> <u>paresthesias</u> and <u>dysesthesias</u> (burning sensation of the feet)

* Enteritis





> [!NOTE]
> Vitamin B5 is pentothenic acid, as in “pente,” the Greek word for “five.”




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Alopecia</u> and dermatitis due to <u>vitamin B<sub>5</sub> deficiency</u> has been observed in animal models in experimental settings. In humans, these features typically occur in severe <u>malnutrition</u> and are likely multifactorial.

---

## Vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>pyridoxine</u>

* Substance class: <u>pyridoxine</u>

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active form: pyridoxal phosphate (<u>PLP</u>)

* Sources: nuts, whole grains, vegetables, <u>yeast</u>, meat (esp. <u>liver</u> and poultry) [[13]](/library/Si0yIf)

* Resorption: cleavage by phosphorylases and subsequent resorption by the intestine

* Transport in blood: partially free, partially bound to <u>albumin</u>





### Functions




* <u>PLP</u> is a <u>coenzyme</u> for the following reactions:

* <u>Transamination</u> (e.g., <u>AST</u> and <u>ALT</u>)

* <u>Decarboxylation</u>

* <u>Amino acid metabolism</u>

* <u>Glycogenolysis</u> (<u>glycogen phosphorylase</u>)

* Involved in the synthesis of:

* <u>Heme</u>

* <u>Histamine</u>

* <u>Niacin</u>

* <u>Glutathione</u>

* <u>Cystathionine</u>

* <u>Neurotransmitters</u>, including:

* <u>Serotonin</u>

* <u>Dopamine</u>

* <u>Epinephrine</u>

* <u>Norepinephrine</u>

* <u>GABA</u>





![Metabolic functions of vitamins B6 and B12](media/subgsb9cpy8m0d2ykun2p8ym.jpg)

Metabolic functions of vitamins B6 and B12

![Section 20.5 Pyridoxine B6](media/small_62f22515a9d1f4.63693134.jpg)

Section 20.5 Pyridoxine B6




### Vitamin B<sub>6</sub> deficiency [[18]](/library/Oi0I7f)




* Causes

* <u>Malnutrition</u>

* <u>Heavy drinking</u>

* <u>Chronic renal failure</u>

* Chronic <u>hepatitis</u>

* <u>Drug interactions</u>

* <u>Isoniazid</u>

* <u>Oral contraceptives</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Cheilosis</u>, <u>glossitis</u>, <u>stomatitis</u>

* <u>Sideroblastic anemia</u>: <u>Vitamin B<sub>6</sub></u> deficiency causes <u>heme synthesis</u> dysfunction with impaired transfer of <u>iron</u> to <u>hemoglobin</u>, which ultimately leads to <u>iron</u> accumulation in <u>RBCs</u>.

* Irritability, <u>seizures</u>, <u>peripheral neuropathy</u>

* <u>Seborrheic dermatitis</u>





![image](media/kzg39p3165l0gr6w3sqh6s44.jpg)




### Vitamin B<sub>6</sub> toxicity




* Causes: : oversupplementation

* Clinical features

* <u>Dizziness</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>

* <u>Peripheral neuropathy</u>

* Dermatosis, <u>photosensitivity</u> [[12]](/library/85YONp)





> [!TIP]
> Although rare, excess <u>pyridoxine</u> can lead to irreversible sensory neuropathy.




### Therapeutic use




* <u>Tuberculosis</u>: administer <u>pyridoxine</u> to prevent <u>INH</u>-induced <u>peripheral neuropathy</u>

* <u>Hyperemesis gravidarum</u>

---

## Vitamin B₇ (biotin)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>biotin</u>

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active form: <u>biotin</u>

* Sources

* Plants (e.g., soy products, nuts), animal products (e.g., <u>liver</u>, egg yolk, dairy products)

* Small amounts are synthesized by intestinal flora

* Resorption: <u>pancreatic enzyme</u> biotinidase cleaves protein-bound <u>biotin</u> into free <u>biotin</u> → active intestinal resorption

* Transport in blood: mainly free





### Functions



* <u>Coenzyme</u> for various carboxylase enzyme complexes, which all add a 1-carbon group

* <u>Fatty acid synthesis</u>: <u>acetyl-CoA carboxylase</u>
* <u>Acetyl-CoA</u> (2C) → <u>malonyl-CoA</u> (3C)

* <u>Gluconeogenesis</u>: <u>pyruvate carboxylase</u>
* <u>Pyruvate</u> (3C) → <u>oxaloacetate</u> (4C)

* <u>Fatty acid</u> reduction: <u>propionyl-CoA carboxylase</u>
* <u>Propionyl-CoA</u> (3C) → <u>methylmalonyl-CoA</u> (4C)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Biotin</u> is a <u>coenzyme</u> in all carboxylase enzyme complexes that are not <u>vitamin K</u>-dependent.




![Section 20.6 Biotin B7](media/small_62f2255fea0bc6.03256356.jpg)

Section 20.6 Biotin B7




### Vitamin B<sub>7</sub> deficiency (<u>biotin deficiency</u>)




* Deficiency is rare

* Causes

* <u>Malnutrition</u>

* Prolonged use of <u>antibiotics</u> (destruction of intestinal flora)

* Excessive consumption of raw egg white: contains avidin → binds <u>biotin</u> in the intestinal lumen → inhibition of <u>biotin</u> resorption

* Clinical features

* Dermatitis

* <u>Conjunctivitis</u>

* Enteritis

* <u>Alopecia</u>

* <u>Myalgia</u>

* Neurological symptoms: <u>lethargy</u>, <u>depression</u>, mental status changes, <u>hallucinations</u>, <u>paresthesia</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Biotin</u> binds to avidin, which is found in raw egg whites: <u>Biotin</u> loves avidin!

---

## Vitamin B₉ (folate)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>folic acid</u>, <u>folate</u>

* Substance class: pteridines

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active form: tetrahydrofolic acid (<u>THF</u>)

* Sources

* Leafy green vegetables, fortified foods (e.g., bread, flour, and cereal)

* Small amounts are synthesized in intestinal flora

* Resorption: <u>jejunum</u> via specific transporters

* Transport in blood: via <u>folate</u>-binding transport <u>proteins</u>

* Storage: small reserve in the <u>liver</u> (enough for approx. 3–4 months)





> [!NOTE]
> Foliage (leafy green vegetables) contains Folate.




### Function



* See “<u>Folate deficiency</u>” for details.




![Section 20.7 Folate B9](media/small_62f2258dba6419.79257262.jpg)

Section 20.7 Folate B9




### <u>Vitamin B<sub>9</sub> deficiency</u> [[19]](/library/Li0wHf)



* See “<u>Folate deficiency</u>” for details.




> [!TIP]
> Unlike <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>, <u>folate deficiency</u> is not associated with neurologic symptoms.




### Therapeutic uses



* Prenatal supplementation (0.4–0.8 mg per day): To reduce the risk of <u>neural tube defects</u>, women should take a <u>folate</u> supplement, starting at least 4 weeks before <u>conception</u> and throughout the <u>first trimester</u> (see “<u>Folic acid supplementation in pregnancy</u>”).

---

## Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>cobalamin</u>

* Substance class: <u>cobalamin</u>

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active forms: methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin (activation occurs in the <u>liver</u>)

* Sources

* Synthesis: Only microorganisms can produce <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u>.

* The <u>colonic</u> flora produces <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u>.

* However, <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> produced by <u>colonic</u> flora cannot be absorbed by the body because the <u>terminal ileum</u> (absorption site) lies prior to the <u>colon</u>.

* Found almost exclusively in animal products (except <u>yeast</u> extract)

* Some dried and fermented plant foods (e.g., tempeh, nori)

* Absorption 

* <u>Stomach</u>: <u>Cobalamin</u> is released from ingested <u>proteins</u> by <u>pepsin</u> and binds to the glycoprotein haptocorrin (<u>R-protein</u>), which protects it from <u>gastric acid</u>.  [[20]](/library/IIXYVz)

* <u>Duodenum</u>: <u>Cobalamin</u> is released from <u>haptocorrin</u> by <u>trypsin</u> and binds to <u>intrinsic factor</u> (IF), a protein produced by the <u>parietal cells</u> of the <u>stomach</u> that facilitates <u>cobalamin</u> absorption in the <u>ileum</u>.

* <u>Terminal ileum</u>: cubilin receptor‐mediated <u>endocytosis</u> of the <u>intrinsic factor</u>-<u>cobalamin</u> complex → breakdown of IF in <u>enterocytes</u>, release of <u>cobalamin</u>, followed by binding to carrier protein transcobalamin II and then enters the plasma → <u>cobalamin</u> is either delivered to metabolically active tissues or stored in the <u>liver</u>

* Transport in blood: via transcobalamin

* Storage: large reserve pool

* 60% in the <u>liver</u> (enough for approx. 3–4 years)

* 30% in <u>muscle tissue</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> is the only water-soluble vitamin that is stored in the body in significant amounts.




![Vitamin B12 absorption](media/zaw3o9nfe5v8uyr2jqfq1ttd.jpg)

Vitamin B12 absorption




### Functions



* <u>Cofactor</u> for enzymes:

* <u>Methionine synthase</u>: Methylcobalamin is required for the transfer of methyl groups (e.g., in <u>DNA synthesis</u>).

* <u>Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase</u> (e.g., in odd-chain <u>fatty acid metabolism</u>)




![Metabolic functions of vitamins B6 and B12](media/subgsb9cpy8m0d2ykun2p8ym.jpg)

Metabolic functions of vitamins B6 and B12

![Methionine cycle](media/mzovqys369921q9zbwx1oc01.jpg)

Methionine cycle

![Section 20.8 Cobalamin B12](media/small_62f225dc846e75.97807312.jpg)

Section 20.8 Cobalamin B12




### <u>Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>



* See “<u>Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>.”




### Therapeutic uses



* Prenatal supplementation for <u>vegetarians</u> (2 μg per day)

## Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)

### Characteristics




* Synonyms: <u>ascorbic acid</u>, ascorbate

* Substance class: lactones

* Inactive precursor (provitamin): none

* Active form: ascorbate

* Sources: fruits and vegetables

* Resorption

* Passive resorption via oral <u>mucosa</u>

* Active resorption in the intestine (especially <u>jejunum</u>)

* Transport in blood: mainly free, only very small amounts as dehydroascorbate

* Storage: no specialized <u>vitamin C</u> stores; high concentrations in organs that require <u>vitamin C</u> as a <u>cofactor</u> (e.g., <u>adrenal gland</u>)





### Functions




* Antioxidant: ascorbate and dehydroascorbate form a redox system 
* Can cause <u>false-negative</u> results on <u>stool guaiac test</u>, which is a color-producing oxidant reaction [[21]](/library/3pXS6_)

* Promotes intestinal <u>iron</u> resorption

* As <u>chelating agent</u>: increases <u>iron</u> solubility through chelate complex formation

* As redox partner: reduces poorly soluble Fe<sup>3+</sup>into highly soluble Fe<sup>2+</sup> → intestinal absorption

* <u>Coenzyme</u> for important enzymatic reactions

* <u>Collagen synthesis</u>: <u>hydroxylation</u> of <u>proline</u> and <u>lysine</u>

* <u>Noradrenaline</u> synthesis: required for <u>dopamine β-hydroxylase</u> (<u>hydroxylation</u> of <u>dopamine</u> to <u>noradrenaline</u>)

* Carnitine synthesis

* <u>Peptide hormone</u> synthesis from prehormones (e.g., <u>vasopressin</u>, <u>calcitonin</u>, <u>oxytocin</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> Think of <u>vitamin C</u> as “absorbic acid” since it promotes the intestinal absorption of <u>iron</u>.




![Section 20.9 Vitamin C](media/small_62f2260ba62163.50118317.jpg)

Section 20.9 Vitamin C




### <u>Vitamin C deficiency</u> [[13]](/library/Si0yIf)




* Causes: severe <u>malnutrition</u> (e.g., due to <u>alcoholism</u>, illicit drug use, and/or psychiatric illness)

* Clinical features

* Scurvy: clinical manifestation of <u>vitamin C</u> deficiency, which leads to impaired <u>collagen synthesis</u> and easily damaged <u>connective tissue</u>

* Follicular hyperkeratosis, perifollicular hemorrhage, coiled “corkscrew” <u>hair</u>

* Subperiosteal hemorrhage

* <u>Gingivitis</u>, swollen <u>gums</u>

* <u>Mucosal</u> bleeding, easy <u>bruising</u>, <u>petechiae</u>

* Impaired <u>wound healing</u>

* <u>Arthralgia</u>, <u>hemarthrosis</u>

* <u>Signs of anemia</u> (fatigue, paleness) ;  [[22]](/library/rIXfVz)

* <u>Normocytic anemia</u>: decreased <u>iron absorption</u> in the <u>small intestine</u>

* <u>Macrocytic anemia</u>: decreased conversion of <u>folate</u> into its active metabolite

* Poor <u>immune response</u>

* Diagnosis: established via measurement of plasma or <u>leukocyte</u> <u>vitamin C</u> levels





![Vitamin C deficiency](media/th5b8qefjbf077f6oxss5lu0.jpg)

Vitamin C deficiency

![Corkscrew hair in scurvy](media/t352tuvkk9ncn8u451736d69.jpg)

Corkscrew hair in scurvy




> [!NOTE]
> Vitamin C deficiency results in sCurvy due to impaired Collagen synthesis.




### Vitamin C toxicity




* Causes: oversupplementation

* Clinical features

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Diarrhea</u>, <u>bloating</u>

* Fatigue

* ↑ Risk of <u>iron toxicity</u> in <u>transfusion</u> patients and <u>hereditary hemochromatosis</u> due to increased absorption of dietary <u>iron</u>

* <u>Nephrolithiasis</u> due to ↑ <u>calcium</u> oxalate formation





### Therapeutic use



* Supportive treatment for <u>methemoglobinemia</u>: <u>Vitamin C</u> reduces Fe<sup>3+</sup> to Fe<sup>2+</sup>
